content.title: About
content.content: Bread stuffing is a ready‑made mixture designed for filling various types of baked goods. It typically contains breadcrumbs, herbs, spices, and sometimes cheese, meat or vegetables, as well as flavor enhancers that give the bread a moist and aromatic taste when baked.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The tradition of stuffing bread with breadcrumbs and herbs dates back to medieval Europe.
Different countries use their own spice blends: Italy favors oregano and basil, France uses rosemary and thyme.
Breadcrumbs help retain moisture, making the interior of the bread softer.
Some versions include dried fruits such as raisins or apricots for sweet breads.
Stuffing mixes are often prepared in advance and can be stored in the refrigerator for up to 5 days.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain breadcrumbs and grain ingredients provide fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Herbs and spices like parsley and basil supply vitamins B1, B2 and B6.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: Most commercial mixes contain little to no added sugar, making them suitable for moderate consumption.

items.title: Supports gut microbiota
items.content: Prebiotic fibers from breadcrumbs can promote the growth of beneficial intestinal bacteria.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: The mix often provides iron and magnesium from whole grains and seeds.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Ready‑made mixes can be salty; people monitoring sodium intake should watch portion sizes.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Some recipes contain dairy, nuts or gluten, which require caution for those with allergies.

items.title: Shelf life
items.content: Because of the breadcrumbs and spices, the mixture can lose flavor and become less safe after prolonged storage.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Certain commercial versions contain food preservatives; homemade versions can be made without them.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Add the stuffing to dough before shaping the loaf or spread it on the surface before baking. It can also be used to fill rolls, croutons, and layered pastries. Typically, only a small amount of water or milk is needed to bring the dry mix to a cohesive consistency.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the unopened package in a cool, dry place, sealed tightly. Once opened, transfer the mixture to an airtight container and store it in the refrigerator for up to 7 days.

chicken-thigh-fried-coated-skin-coating-.title: Chicken thigh, fried, coated, skin not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Fried chicken thigh coated in a crispy breading. The skin and coating are not consumed, only the meat of the thigh. Served at restaurant (852) and is a popular source of protein and energy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Deep‑frying creates a golden crust while keeping the interior juicy.
Chicken thighs contain more fat than breast meat, making them more flavorful when fried.
Traditional breading often combines flour, spices, and sometimes breadcrumbs.
In some cuisines the skin is removed before frying to reduce calories.
The dish is commonly served with sauces such as barbecue, honey‑mustard, or garlic aioli.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken thigh provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat contains niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Chicken supplies iron, zinc, and phosphorus, important for blood formation and bone health.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The fat in the thigh offers sustained satiety and a quick energy source.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: Proper cooking makes the proteins readily available for digestion.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Fried meat contains a notable amount of saturated fat, which may raise cholesterol levels if eaten frequently.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The dish is calorie‑rich; portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑loss diets.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: A small number of people may be allergic to chicken proteins.

items.title: Trans fats in breading
items.content: If pre‑made breading mixes are used, they can contain trans fats.

items.title: Salt and spices
items.content: Excessive salt in the coating may be unsuitable for individuals with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Consume only the thigh meat, avoiding the skin and breading. Pair the dish with vegetable sides, mashed potatoes, or whole‑grain products. To reduce calories, blot excess oil with a paper towel before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cooked dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat in the oven or skillet to restore crispness. Do not keep at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: The Burger King hamburger is a classic fast‑food item featuring a beef patty, melted cheese, pickles, fresh vegetables, and the signature sauce, served in a soft bun.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first Burger King hamburger was introduced in 1954 under the name “Whopper”.
The patty is cooked on an open grill, giving it a distinctive smoky flavor.
Local variations may include regional ingredients, such as pineapple in Asian markets.
Burger King offers a plant‑based version – the Impossible Whopper – with a veggie patty.
There is a “King Burger” challenge item weighing over 1.5 kg, sold in limited promotions.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The beef patty provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Red meat contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: The hamburger supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc contributes to immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: Combining protein, fat, and carbohydrates, the burger quickly replenishes energy stores.

items.title: High calorie and fat content
items.content: A typical hamburger can exceed 500 kcal and contain a notable amount of saturated fat, which may be undesirable in excess.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Sauces and processed ingredients add sodium, potentially affecting blood pressure.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Ingredients may include dairy, gluten, and soy, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Trans fats
items.content: Some preparation methods use oils that contain trans fats, which are harmful to cardiovascular health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hamburgers are typically eaten by hand, optionally adding ketchup, mustard, or mayo. You can split it in half for easier handling and pair it with fries or a side salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best consumed immediately. If needed, store in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours, wrapped in food‑grade film. Reheat using an oven or microwave to retain bun texture.

lettuce-salad-with-avocado-tomato-and-or.title: Lettuce Salad with Avocado, Tomato, and Carrots

content.title: About
content.content: The “Lettuce” salad is a mix of leafy lettuce, ripe avocado, fresh tomato, and grated carrot. Other vegetables may be added optionally, but no dressing is used, preserving the natural flavors of the ingredients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Leafy lettuce is high in water content, helping to keep the body hydrated.
Avocado provides monounsaturated fats that are heart‑healthy.
Tomatoes are a rich source of lycopene, a powerful antioxidant.
Carrots are loaded with beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
The lack of dressing makes the salad low‑calorie and suitable for diet plans.

items.title: Supports Vision
items.content: Beta‑carotene from carrots and vitamin A promote eye health.

items.title: Heart Health
items.content: Monounsaturated fats in avocado help lower LDL cholesterol.

items.title: Antioxidant Protection
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes and vitamin E from lettuce protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Hydration and Fiber
items.content: High water and fiber content aid digestion and increase satiety.

items.title: Immune Support
items.content: Vitamins C and K present in the salad strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Avocado Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to avocado.

items.title: Pesticide Residues
items.content: If the vegetables are not organic, pesticide residues may be present; thorough washing is recommended.

items.title: Digestive Discomfort
items.content: Large amounts of raw vegetables can cause gas in sensitive people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad fresh as a standalone dish or as a side. Optionally add a squeeze of lemon, a pinch of salt, or your favorite herbs for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours to maintain crispness.

pizza-extra-cheese-thin-crust.title: Pizza with Extra Cheese, Thin Crust

content.title: About
content.content: Pizza with extra cheese and a thin crust is a classic Italian dish featuring a crisp, slender base topped with tomato sauce, generous melted cheese, and a variety of optional toppings. The extra cheese adds richness and a satisfying stretch.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Thin‑crust pizza originated in Naples in the early 20th century as a lighter alternative to the traditional Neapolitan style.
Mozzarella is the traditional cheese, but many pizzerias boost flavor with cheddar, parmesan, or a blend of cheeses.
Pizza was the first food delivered to space, aboard the Russian Mir station in 2001.
In the United States, extra‑cheese pizza ranks among the top‑5 most ordered pizza variants in chain restaurants.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Cheese provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle repair and growth.

items.title: Calcium for bones
items.content: Dairy cheese is rich in calcium, supporting strong bones and teeth.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Tomato sauce and cheese supply B2 and B12 vitamins, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Lycopene in tomato sauce
items.content: Tomatoes contain lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that helps protect cells from oxidative damage.

items.title: Quick energy
items.content: The combination of thin crust and cheese offers a fast‑acting source of carbohydrates and fats, useful before physical activity.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Abundant cheese and crust make the pizza calorie‑dense, so it should be enjoyed in moderation.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Cheese contains saturated fats, which can raise cholesterol levels if consumed excessively.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People sensitive to lactose may experience digestive discomfort after eating.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Cheese and sauce often contain added salt; individuals with hypertension should watch portion sizes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pizza hot, sliced into individual pieces. Fresh herbs such as basil or oregano, or a light side salad, complement the richness of the extra cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in an oven or grill to restore the crisp crust.
